nesnd_small_states.2.far_south: More and more cargo ships are crossing the sea between Australia and New Zealand. The ports can afford to hire dockhands, the interior has found buyers for its produce, and the Far South no longer lives off a single source of wealth.\n\nFarmers and labourers have a surer living, and the government's revenue has grown with it. The schools and local services of the years ahead will depend on the goods carried over this sea, and on the people who produce them.
nesnd_small_states.2.burma: Upriver at $STATE_MANDALAY$ and downriver at $STATE_PEGU$, industries have found their feet. Transport carries the produce of both to market, and farmers, labourers and merchants all have money coming in.\n\nNow that taxes have somewhere to come from, offices and schools are more than talk. But how that money is shared out, upriver and downriver each have their own reckoning.
nesnd_small_states.2.siam: Trade between Bangkok and the outer provinces has settled into a steady course. The crowded, wealthy capital needs what the provinces produce; the provincial workshops and estates, with a market at last, can pay wages and pay their taxes.\n\nOnce money reached the treasury, the hands held out for it soon followed: the army wants its pay, and the provinces want schools and funds for public business. Those who earned this revenue for the country now expect the country to do something for their lives in return.
nesnd_small_states.6.far_south: The production and shipping of Australia and New Zealand can now pay for public affairs in both. The offices are staffed and the schools are open; the Far South earns its own money and trains its own people.\n\nThe government stands a little straighter when it deals with foreign powers. The wealth these communities have built is the ground on which the Far South claims its independence.
nesnd_small_states.6.burma: Production, transport and public business have found firm footing upriver and downriver at $STATE_PEGU$. The treasury has an income, local people are serving as officials and teachers, and the two halves of the country now exchange far more than goods.\n\nBurma can run its own affairs on these savings. When foreign powers make their next demand, the court will have both money and men behind it.
nesnd_small_states.6.siam: Production in Bangkok and the outer provinces can now pay for public business, and administration, schools and defence all have something to stand on. Little by little, the treasury's income is turning into the means for Siam to stand alone.\n\nMore money has brought more quarrels. The provinces want schools and public works, the army wants its pay on time, and the capital has bills of its own. The argument is no longer only about where the money comes from, but about what kind of Siam it should build.
nesnd_small_livelihood_journal_reason: A small country's independence rests on the ordinary family's rice bowl. Only when farmers can pay their taxes, labourers can find work and merchants can carry goods to a buyer can the government afford its officials, schools and soldiers. If those who produce are crushed under rent, debt and idleness, every great affair of state can only be squeezed out of them.\n\nForeign capital brings money and know-how, and the overlord is willing to carry part of the load. But to be heard among these powers, the country's industries must run on their own, and its people must learn new skills.
nesnd_small_economy_journal_reason: The treasury's money comes from what the people produce, and the producers must first feed themselves. Farmers must sell their harvest, artisans and labourers need work, and goods must get over the roads and onto the ships before they reach a buyer. Let any link stay blocked for long, and poverty passes all the way down the chain.\n\nWe start with the industries we already have. Once the workshops can hire people and turn a profit, households can put something by, and only then can the country speak of the future.
nesnd_small_governance_journal_reason: Now that industry earns an income, the provinces are short of people who can get things done. Collecting taxes, running public business and teaching children cannot depend for ever on favours from a few acquaintances. Teachers and clerks need salaries paid on time, and students need to see where their learning will take them.\n\nAt least part of the taxes people hand over ought to come back to them as schools and public offices they can use.
nesnd_small_regional_economy_journal_rea: The crowded, wealthy places need the produce of other regions, and the farms, mines, fisheries, forests and workshops of those regions need bigger markets. While producers and buyers stay apart, no amount of wealth in the ground will put money in the inhabitants' pockets.\n\nProduction must be built up in both regions, and the road between them opened. Regions with different produce can trade what each lacks; those with similar trades can divide the work. Keep the business going long enough, and neither region can do without the other.
nesnd_small_regional_governance_journal_: Goods already move between the two regions, but the people who run public affairs cannot all crowd into one place. Taxes are raised in both, so offices and schools must take root in both. Otherwise, the more the provinces produce, the more of their business must be referred to someone far away.\n\nThe country needs people to do the work, and schools to train those who will follow them. When local people can take on new posts, the country need no longer search the same few cities for every capable hand.
nesnd_small_order_journal_reason: Independence, or broad autonomy, means deciding many things for ourselves, and carrying the burden of trade and defence on our own shoulders. The people want to be free of outside meddling; even more, they want their lives to get better.\n\nThe workshops need materials and buyers, the provinces need schools and officials, and the army must be paid. Only if the country's own resources can bear all this will self-rule be more than a phrase.
nesnd_small_dispute_journal_reason: When life becomes unbearable, people in the provinces band together to find a way out. Some want new rules for land and hired labour; others want a say in national affairs. Hardships once suffered behind each family's closed door have become the demands of a movement.\n\nPermit them to organise, promise legislation, or call in the police: whatever the government does, landlords, employers and those who want change will all see whose side it is on.
nesnd_small_public_desc: Offices and workshops alike lack people who can read and have a trade. Spend a year of public funds teaching residents new occupations.
nesnd_small_specialise_button_desc: Merchants and guilds want to grow their business within the market we already belong to. Follow the existing trade routes and find more buyers for local goods.
nesnd_small_own_market_button_desc: Open a market of our own, and keep materials, production and sales in our own hands.
nesnd_small_order_button_desc: Now that we govern ourselves, our laws, market, public business and defence are ours alone to run.
nesnd_small_request_autonomy_desc: We can collect our own taxes and staff our own offices. It is time the overlord handed more of our affairs back to us.
nesnd_small_request_independence_desc: Negotiate with the overlord and end our subordination with dignity, taking full charge of our own affairs at home and abroad.
nesnd_small_request_market_desc: Ask the owner of our market to let us set up on our own, running supply, demand and transport ourselves.
nesnd_small_states.2.d: Our industries have begun to give farmers and labourers a steady way to make a living. Goods find buyers, employers can pay wages, and more and more households live by their own work.\n\nWith these households settled, the treasury has a tax base it can count on.
nesnd_small_states.3.d: The offices and schools are open at last, and they can be kept open. Public business has people to handle it, books have teachers, and the workshops are starting to find hands who can read and know a trade.\n\nThe more people read, the more clearly they can say what they want from their government.
nesnd_small_states.4.d: We have changed markets, and the temporary deals that merchants and companies struck under the old one have lapsed. Materials, customers and transport must all be found again in the new market.\n\nThe government can change course in a moment; the producers' goods are still sitting in their warehouses.
nesnd_small_states.5.d: Years have gone by, and law, trade and local industry have still not managed to carry our programme of self-government. The workshops and schools we built go on working, but the conditions the state needs have never all come together.\n\nThe undertaking must be set aside for now. When the conditions are met, it can be taken up again.
nesnd_small_states.6.d: Local industry can pay for schools and offices, and our markets and defences are enough to stand on our own. With people and money in hand, the government has more to bargain with when it deals with foreign powers.\n\nThese savings were built up by the people, tax by tax and day's work by day's work.
nesnd_small_states.11.d: The government has carried out the legal reform it promised the provinces. Those who organised for it now know they can move national policy. What they once had to swallow, they can now challenge in the name of the law.\n\nThe masters who lost by it will not let the matter rest. The new law is on the books; now someone has to enforce it.
nesnd_small_states.10.land: Farmers and labourers in the provinces are struggling, and the land reform movement is gaining support. Who owns the land and who commands the labour decide how much they keep after a year's toil, and whether they can ever be free of their old masters.\n\nThose who want change have organised. If we tell them to keep enduring, why should they go on believing in this order?
nesnd_small_states.10.labor: Labourers' lives are growing harder, and the labour movement has won hearts in the provinces. Workers want to bargain over pay, hours and safety at work, and no longer face their employers one by one. To the employers, these demands strike at their profits and at their command over their workers.
nesnd_small_states.10.representation: Local liberal and radical movements are rallying support. Those shut out by birth or political qualification want a say in the affairs that rule their lives; those already inside are in no hurry to make room for them.\n\nThey have organised, and the argument can no longer be kept on paper.
nesnd_small_states.20.autonomy: The government of [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] cites the progress of its economy and administration as grounds for running more of its own affairs. By its account, it can bear these responsibilities, and the overlord's restrictions ought to be loosened.\n\nIf we agree, its autonomy will rise one step.
nesnd_small_states.20.independence: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] asks to negotiate an end to its subordination, with its own government taking charge of affairs at home and abroad, and the two countries remaining at peace after independence.\n\nWhat they want this time is to decide their country's future for themselves. To agree is to give up our overlordship, and with it the quarrels we might fight to keep it.
nesnd_small_states.20.market: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] asks to set up a separate market and run its own production and trade. Its merchants would arrange their own materials and buyers, and the existing flow of goods between our countries would change with it.
nesnd_small_states.20.defence: [SCOPE.sCountry('canon_sender').GetName] asks for a defensive treaty with our country. They want an ally they can count on.\n\nOnce the treaty is signed, an attack on them may draw our army into war.
nesnd_small_states.21.d: The government means to propose a common defence to [SCOPE.sCountry('small_receiver').GetName]. Our countries are on good terms and our borders lie close; if our armies can support each other, an aggressor will have to think twice.\n\nThe envoy's letter is already drafted.
